component_records.title: Programme governance, compliance and RFP obligations
component_records.description: A single compliance workstream owns every contractual and commercial obligation in the RFP. Submission of the proposal constitutes the Vendor's acknowledgment and acceptance of all RFP terms, conditions, exhibits and attachments (R009), and we will not refer to any terms and conditions other than the City's, so the proposal cannot be rejected as non-responsive on that ground (R122). We will notify the City in writing of any known or reasonably knowable RFP error before the submission date and accept that we bid at our own risk and receive no additional compensation or time for such errors (R114), and we will acknowledge and incorporate all addenda, accepting that failure to do so does not relieve us of any term or condition (R116). All data, materials and documentation originated and prepared for the City under this solicitation are acknowledged to be the City's property (R037). We will provide a certification of insurance before any work commences (R123) and an underwriter's endorsement with additional insured verbiage from a surety admitted in the State of Washington (R124). Proposal development costs are borne entirely by the Vendor and not charged to the City (R117). The compliance workstream also runs the RFP question process: all Vendor questions about the RFP are submitted in writing to the City by the August 28, 2024 deadline, logged with the answer received on September 5, 2024, and traced into the proposal so that every clarification is reflected in the response (R027). The programme is governed by a joint steering committee (City sponsor, Vendor engagement director), a monthly status report against the phase plan, a risk and issue log, and a change-control board, with City sign-off gates at the end of each phase.

component_records.title: Discovery, fit-gap and phased implementation plan
component_records.description: Phase 0 (March–May 2025) is a structured discovery and fit-gap against the City's completed Requirements document, producing a confirmed module scope, a process-improvement register and a signed-off phase plan. The replacement ERP is implemented in three phases — Phase 1 financials core (General Ledger, Budget, Purchasing, Accounts Payable, Accounts Receivable), Phase 2 extended financials and revenue (Project and Grant Accounting, Capital Assets, Contract Management, Enterprise Cashiering, ACFR reporting), Phase 3 HCM (Human Resources, Time and Attendance, Payroll) — with each phase's go-live sequenced so that all modules in scope are live by January 1, 2027 (R011, R030). The plan runs from March 2025 through January 2027 and is baselined at contract signature, with the City's approval gate on any change to phasing (R029). The solution delivers the integrated ERP modules and functionality defined in the Requirements document issued with the RFP (R010) and satisfies the City's functional and technical requirements as rated line by line in that document (R004). Discovery explicitly adopts the Vendor's standard best practices rather than replicating current City practice, with each proposed process change recorded, agreed with the process owner and reflected in configuration and training.

component_records.title: Financials suite: General Ledger, Budget, Purchasing, Payables, Receivables, Projects and Grants, Capital Assets, Cashiering and ACFR
component_records.description: The core financial suite replaces the Eden General Ledger, Purchasing, Contract Management, Accounts Payable, Accounts Receivable, Project and Grant Accounting and Capital Assets functions with native ERP modules, configured to the City's chart of accounts, approval hierarchies and grant compliance rules (R013). Budget is delivered as a native ERP budgeting module with position, worksheet and multi-year modelling, replacing the Excel-based Budget process (R016), and ACFR reporting is delivered through the ERP's financial reporting and disclosure tooling with a configured ACFR report pack, replacing the Excel-based ACFR workpapers (R017). Enterprise Cashiering is delivered as a native ERP cashiering module with cash drawer, receipting and reconciliation controls, replacing Quadrant (R015). All financial modules are configured out of the box wherever possible; any modification is rated 2 in the Requirements document with its estimated cost stated (R106).

component_records.title: Human Capital Management: Human Resources, Time and Attendance and Payroll
component_records.description: HCM is delivered as part of the same ERP suite — Human Resources, Time and Attendance and Payroll — replacing the Eden HR, time and attendance and payroll functions rather than integrating to them (R014). Because HCM is native to the ERP, employee, position, pay and labour-distribution data flow to the General Ledger without an interface, and the solution is offered as an integrated suite rather than a best-of-breed HCM, so no separate HCM-to-ERP integration demonstration is required (R006). Payroll is configured for the City's pay cycles, bargaining-unit rules, deduction and accrual structures, and time and attendance for its shift, leave and overtime policies, with the retained Power Time police scheduling feed handled in the integration component.

component_records.title: Integration platform and interfaces to retained systems
component_records.description: A managed integration layer (published APIs, scheduled file exchange and an integration monitoring console) connects the ERP to the systems the City retains. Interfaces are built and tested for NeoGov recruiting (R018), Power Time police scheduling and time and attendance (R019), Amanda permitting, planning and land management (R020), MyBuildingPermit.com (R021), RecTrac parks and recreation (R022) and Class for the Dumas Bay Conference Center (R023). For OpenGov and SharePoint we deliver a documented interface feasibility assessment with a recommendation and, where the City approves it, a configured interface (R024). For the Excel shadow systems for Enterprise Asset Management and Fleet Management we deliver a disposition assessment covering replace, integrate or retain, with a costed recommendation for each, and implement the agreed option (R026). Every interface is specified in an interface control document, tested in a dedicated integration test cycle and covered by post-go-live monitoring.

component_records.title: Data conversion, report development, testing and training
component_records.description: Data conversion covers each replaced system — Eden financials and HCM, Quadrant cashiering, and the Excel Budget and ACFR workbooks — with a conversion methodology, per-module conversion specifications stating years and data elements, mock conversions, reconciliation and City sign-off before cutover. Report development delivers the City's operational and statutory reports, including the ACFR report pack, through the ERP's reporting toolset, with a report inventory agreed in discovery. Testing follows a documented methodology and toolset: unit, integration, conference-room pilot, user acceptance and parallel payroll testing, with defect tracking and exit criteria per phase. Training combines role-based instructor-led sessions, sandbox environments and quick-reference guides, supported by a change-management plan that names process owners, communication cadence and readiness assessments. All of these services are included in the implementation price for go-live.

component_records.title: Pricing submission: Exhibit A, deployment options and assumptions
component_records.description: The Pricing Summary in Exhibit A is completed in full as Section 3 of the proposal, showing costs for software and implementation services (R057). Pricing is comprehensive, including all taxes and all available discounts applied to the quoted prices (R058), and is held valid for 180 days from the response date (R059). The price includes every implementation service required for go-live — software deployment, data conversion, system configuration, report development, testing and training (R061) — and ongoing license/subscription and maintenance for Years 1 through 10 (R062). Pricing is sized at 130 named and 85 concurrent financial users (R128) and 400 FTEs and 744 W2s for HCM (R129). Year 1 software costs are itemized for General Ledger, Budget, Project and Grant Accounting, Purchasing and Contract Management, Accounts Payable, Accounts Receivable, Capital Assets and Enterprise Cashiering (R130) and for Human Resources, Time and Attendance and Payroll (R131). A separate pricing sheet is provided for each deployment option offered — hosted/SaaS and on-premises — so the City can compare like for like (R127), and every priced line carries a stated assumption in the Assumptions column (R134).

component_records.title: Demo, references and vendor qualification
component_records.description: We will present the functional and technical product demonstration to the City following the pre-defined Demo Script issued to finalists (R032) and will demonstrate the product meeting the City's functional and technical requirements line by line, since script adherence and demonstrated fit are scored (R034). Our references are submitted on the Exhibit B forms with three current and two prior customers for the proposed software, each with customer name, employee count, population, contact name and title, telephone and email, software scope, implementation duration, go-live date and reason for change (R093, R136), and we prioritise Washington State public-sector references of comparable size and scope (R094). We disclose any contract terminated for convenience, non-performance or any other reason, and any legal action with a customer, in the past five years, naming the contracting party and address (R095). Our qualification rests on successful implementations for cities of similar size and scope of services (R005), evidenced by those references.

component_records.title: Hosted platform, security and support operations
component_records.description: The ERP is hosted in the Vendor's SaaS environment with a priced on-premises alternative, and the proposal's technology and security overviews describe the architecture options, data centre locations and redundancy, hardware specifications, mobile hardware and OS options, remote access, integration tools and update scheduling, and the security model, standards, SSO/SAML administration, multi-factor authentication and breach communication, response and cost. Support is delivered under a documented SLA with support hours, guaranteed response times, named resources and an escalation path, baseline and premium tiers compared, user groups and conferences, post-go-live tools, backup strategy and disaster recovery covering backup, redundancy and location. This component carries the platform and support narrative that the RFP's technology and support sections require; it is priced within the Exhibit A pricing sheets.

finding_verdicts.label: R036 <-> R042: Proposals must not exceed 100 pages, excluding a Vendor sample contract. / The response must include one electronic PDF copy of the entire RFP proposal in the order defined in the table, not exceeding 100 total pages excluding sample contracts provided.

items.text: The City of Federal Way, Washington, issued this RFP on August 16, 2024 for ERP software and implementation services.

Federal Way incorporated in February 1990 and changed from a council-manager to a mayor-council form of government in November 2010, and today has an estimated 22,485 people employed within its city limits.

The City's current ERP landscape is Eden for General Ledger, Purchasing, Contract Management, Accounts Payable, Accounts Receivable, Project and Grant Accounting, Capital Assets, Human Resources, Time and Attendance and Payroll, Quadrant for Cashiering, and Excel spreadsheets for Budget and ACFR — all designated for replacement.

The City will retain and integrate NeoGov (Recruiting), Power Time (Police scheduling and time and attendance), Amanda and MyBuildingPermit.com (permitting, planning, land management), RecTrac (Parks and Recreation), Class (Dumas Bay Conference Center), OpenGov and SharePoint, with OpenGov and SharePoint interfaces still to be reviewed.
Excel shadow systems for Enterprise Asset Management and Fleet Management are under review with the interface to be determined, while SeeClick Fix (311) and Esri (GIS) are retained with no interface.
The City wants process improvement through implementing new systems and intends to adopt the best practices offered by the selected Vendor rather than replicate current practices.
The City seeks a Vendor with experience successfully implementing the proposed solutions for cities of similar size and scope of services.
The City intends to purchase an integrated ERP solution covering the modules and functionality defined in the Requirements document issued with the RFP.
The City expects the replacement ERP to be implemented in a phased approach, or as otherwise recommended by the selected Vendor and approved by the City.
The City is also open to best-of-breed Human Capital Management proposals, provided the HCM solution can integrate with the selected ERP system.

The financial scope covers General Ledger, Budget, Project and Grant Accounting, Purchasing and Contract Management, Accounts Payable, Accounts Receivable, Capital Assets and Enterprise Cashiering, and the HCM scope covers Human Resources, Time and Attendance and Payroll.
Implementation services must cover go-live including software deployment, data conversion, system configuration, report development, testing and training, plus integration and travel.

The planned implementation window runs from March 2025 to January 2027, following finalist selection in October 2024, demos in December 2024, due diligence in January 2025 and contract negotiations from January 2025.
Pricing must include software license/subscription and maintenance costs for Years 1 through 10, with a separate pricing sheet for each deployment option offered (e.g., SaaS or on-premises).
Proposals are scored on weighted criteria: Software 30, Implementation 25, Technology 15, Vendor 15 and Cost Value 15.
The Implementation criterion requires Go Live for all modules in scope by January 1, 2027.

Finalists must present functional and technical product demos to the City following a pre-defined Demo Script, and demos are judged on adherence to the script and on demonstrating the product meeting the City's functional and technical requirements.

Every requirement line item must be rated on the scale 4 (standard/out of the box or configuration), 3 (third-party software integrated, named), 2 (modification, with estimated cost), 0 (not available) or F (future release, with month and year), with a comment of no more than 100 words per item.
Applications missing a significant number of required features and technology preferences may be eliminated, and blank requirement responses may cause a proposal to be rejected as incomplete.
Vendor questions are due August 28, 2024 at 3:00 p.m. PT, answers are posted September 5, 2024, and proposals are due September 17, 2024 at 3:00 p.m. PT, with late submissions not considered.
The City may award based solely on the initial proposal without discussion, so proposals must be submitted initially on the most favorable terms available.
No contract will be awarded until it is approved by City Council.

Proposals must be emailed to Thuch.Mam@FederalWayWA.gov as a single electronic PDF of no more than 100 pages (sample contracts excluded), plus one completed Requirements document in MS Word format without format changes.

The proposal must follow the prescribed five-section structure — Cover Letter (max two pages), Requirements, Pricing, Implementation and Support — and responses deviating from the requested format may be classified non-responsive and disqualified.
Marketing literature must not be included in the proposal, and hyperlinks or cross-references to other line items are not allowed in the Requirements responses.

Pricing must be comprehensive including all taxes and available discounts and valid for 180 days from the response date, sized at 130 named and 85 concurrent financial users and 400 FTEs and 744 W2s for HCM.

The Technology overview must address hosted, on-premises and SaaS architecture options, data center locations and redundancy, hardware specifications, mobile hardware and OS options, remote access, integration tools and methodologies, and software update scheduling.

The Security overview must cover the security model and standards, security administration including SSO and SAML, multi-factor authentication, and security breach customer communication, response and cost.

Vendors must supply three current and two prior customer references on the Exhibit B forms, preferably Washington State public sector clients, and disclose any contract terminated for convenience or non-performance or any legal action with a customer in the past five years.

The ERP Requirements document is issued as a separate Word document that vendors must obtain and complete as Section 2 of the proposal, and sample contract documents (Statement of Work, license agreement, maintenance/support agreements, SLAs) must be submitted with any exceptions to the RFP documented.
Vendor questions are due August 28, 2024 at 3:00 p.m. PT and answers are posted September 5, 2024.
The City's current ERP landscape is Eden for financials and HCM, Quadrant for cashiering, and Excel for Budget and ACFR, all designated for replacement.
The planned implementation window runs from March 2025 to January 2027, following finalist selection in October 2024 and contract negotiations from January 2025.

The City's current ERP landscape is Eden for General Ledger, Purchasing, Contract Management, Accounts Payable, Accounts Receivable, Project and Grant Accounting, Capital Assets, Human Resources, Time and Attendance and Payroll, Quadrant for Cashiering, and Excel spreadsheets for Budget and ACFR — all designated for replacement.
The City is open to best-of-breed HCM proposals provided the HCM solution can integrate with the selected ERP system.
The City will retain and integrate NeoGov, Power Time, Amanda, MyBuildingPermit.com, RecTrac, Class, OpenGov and SharePoint, with the OpenGov and SharePoint interfaces still to be reviewed.
Excel shadow systems for Enterprise Asset Management and Fleet Management are under review with the interface to be determined.
Pricing must be sized at 130 named and 85 concurrent financial users and 400 FTEs and 744 W2s for HCM.
Pricing must include software license/subscription and maintenance costs for Years 1 through 10, with a separate pricing sheet for each deployment option offered.
The City seeks a Vendor with experience successfully implementing the proposed solutions for cities of similar size and scope of services.
Finalists must present functional and technical product demos following a pre-defined Demo Script, judged on adherence to the script and on demonstrating the product meeting the City's requirements.

The Requirements document issued separately with the RFP is assumed to define the full functional and technical scope, and the solution is scoped and priced against it rather than against any narrower module list.

The three-phase sequence (financials core, extended financials and revenue, then HCM) is assumed acceptable to the City as the Vendor-recommended alternative to an undefined phasing, subject to City approval at the Phase 0 gate.
January 1, 2027 is treated as a firm contractual go-live deadline for all modules in scope, not merely a scored evaluation factor, and no partial go-live is proposed as the end state.

HR, Time and Attendance, Payroll, Cashiering, Budget and ACFR are assumed to be delivered as native ERP modules rather than as integrations to third-party products, since the RFP leaves the choice open.

Enterprise Asset Management and Fleet Management are assumed to be in scope for assessment and, if the City elects replacement, for configuration, with the interface cost carried as a priced option rather than a firm line.
OpenGov and SharePoint are assumed to require a feasibility assessment and recommendation as the deliverable, with interface build priced only if the City approves it.
The demo script is assumed to be issued to finalists with the notification e-mail, and the demo is prepared against the City's completed Requirements document in the interim.
The 100-page cap is treated as mandatory for the PDF proposal, with the completed Requirements document in MS Word submitted as a separate file outside that count.
The 100-word limit is assumed to apply to the comment text of each requirement row, with the rating code excluded from the count.
Discounts are assumed to be applied to the quoted prices in Exhibit A rather than merely disclosed, so the City sees net pricing.
Two deployment options are assumed to be required — hosted/SaaS and on-premises — and each is priced on its own sheet.
Project and Grant Accounting is assumed to be a single priced line item despite appearing twice in the template, and the duplication is flagged to the City in writing before submission.

The insurance certification and underwriter's endorsement are assumed to be satisfied by the Vendor's standard public-entity coverage with the City named as additional insured, with limits confirmed at contract negotiation.

Items rated 2 or F in the Requirements document are assumed to be acceptable responses provided the modification cost or release month and year is stated, and are not treated as firm committed deliverables unless the City accepts them in the contract.
The reference fields 'Employee Count' and 'Population' are assumed to mean the reference customer's own workforce and the population of the jurisdiction it serves.
Three current and two prior references are assumed to be the required minimum, with additional references supplied only if they strengthen the submission.

The August 28, 2024 question deadline is assumed to be firm and to be met by written submission to the City's designated contact, with answers received on September 5, 2024 treated as the only clarifications available before the September 17, 2024 proposal deadline.

Requirements document not in hand, so scope and price rest on an unseen document. The functional and technical scope is defined by a separate Requirements document that the bidder must obtain, complete and submit as Section 2, and the proposal is priced against it. If that document is larger, more detailed or more demanding than assumed, the fixed implementation price and the January 1, 2027 schedule are both wrong, and the bidder carries the difference. The City may also treat the completed document as a binding contractual commitment. The RFP issues the Requirements document separately and the solution explicitly scopes and prices against it rather than a module list; the document is not available at the time of writing, so the price is built on an unverified scope.

January 1, 2027 go-live treated as firm for all modules. The RFP states the go-live date only as an Implementation evaluation criterion, but the proposed solution treats it as a firm contractual deadline for every module with no partial go-live as an end state. If the City enforces it contractually, any slippage in Phase 1 cascades into HCM and payroll cutover, and the bidder faces liquidated damages or a disputed acceptance. The window is roughly 22 months from March 2025 for three phases, six retained-system interfaces and a payroll parallel run. The RFP leaves the status of the date open, and the solution has chosen the strictest reading; the schedule covers three phases, six interfaces and payroll testing in under two years.

Native HCM and payroll replacement carries the highest delivery risk. The solution replaces Eden HR, Time and Attendance and Payroll with native ERP modules configured to bargaining-unit rules, deduction and accrual structures and shift, leave and overtime policies, plus a Power Time police scheduling feed. Payroll errors at go-live are highly visible to 400 FTEs and 744 W2s and can trigger grievance or statutory exposure. The RFP left the choice between integration and native modules open, and the solution chose the harder path. Payroll replacement with parallel testing is the most failure-prone part of any ERP programme, and the solution has taken on native payroll rather than integrating a proven HCM product.

Enterprise Asset Management and Fleet Management disposition unresolved. The RFP marks the Excel shadow systems for Enterprise Asset Management and Fleet Management as under review with the interface to be determined. The solution prices only an assessment plus a costed option, so if the City elects replacement or a full interface, that work is unplanned and unpriced inside a fixed-price engagement. It also affects the data conversion and report inventory. The RFP explicitly leaves the treatment open, and the solution carries the interface cost as a priced option rather than a firm line, so the default outcome is a scope gap.

Phasing and best-practice adoption undefined, so the plan may not match City expectations. The RFP allows a phased approach or any alternative the Vendor recommends and the City approves, and separately expects the City to adopt the Vendor's best practices, without defining approval criteria or what best-practice commitments must be proposed. The proposed three-phase sequence and its process-change register could be rejected at the Phase 0 gate, forcing re-planning and re-pricing after contract signature. Best-practice-driven process change also raises City staff resistance and training effort that is easy to underprice. Both the phasing and the best-practice obligation are left to Vendor recommendation and City approval, and the solution's phase plan is an inference rather than a City requirement.

OpenGov and SharePoint interface scope ambiguous. For OpenGov and SharePoint the RFP says the interface is to be reviewed rather than confirmed. The solution delivers only a feasibility assessment and recommendation, with the build priced only if the City approves it. If the City reads the requirement as a firm interface obligation, the bid is non-responsive or the build is absorbed at the bidder's cost. The RFP's 'Review' status leaves the deliverable open, and the solution has chosen the narrower reading of assessment only.

Six retained-system interfaces depend on third-party cooperation. The solution commits to building and testing interfaces to NeoGov, Power Time, Amanda, MyBuildingPermit.com, RecTrac and Class. Each depends on the third-party vendor's API, documentation and willingness to support testing, none of which the City or the bidder controls. A single uncooperative vendor can delay an integration test cycle and push a phase go-live. Six mandatory interfaces are required by the RFP and the solution commits to a dedicated integration test cycle for each, but the RFP gives no information on those vendors' interface capabilities.

100-page cap and conflicting page-limit wording. The RFP states the page limit twice with different wording, and the solution treats the 100-page cap as mandatory for the PDF while submitting the Requirements document in Word outside the count. If the City counts the Word document or reads the cap differently, a compliant proposal could be disqualified as non-responsive, or the bid team could cut content that is scored. R036 and R042 conflict on what is excluded from the 100 pages, and the treatment of the Word Requirements document is an assumption in the solution rather than a stated RFP rule.

Proposal structure and section order not available. The RFP requires the proposal to follow the order defined in a table that is not included, and deviations may be classified non-responsive. The bid team must guess the section order for a five-section proposal with a two-page cover letter, and a wrong order risks disqualification regardless of content quality. The ordering table is referenced but absent, and the RFP states that format deviations may render a proposal non-responsive.

Demo script not issued, yet demo adherence is scored. Demos are judged on adherence to a pre-defined script that is not included in the RFP and is issued only to finalists. The solution assumes the script arrives with the finalist notification and prepares against the Requirements document in the interim. If the script covers modules or scenarios the bid team did not prepare, the demo score suffers on a criterion worth 25 points. The script is a referenced document that is not in the RFP, and the solution's preparation approach is an assumption about when it will arrive.

Insurance and endorsement requirements stated without limits. The RFP requires a certification of insurance and an underwriter's endorsement with additional insured wording from a surety admitted in Washington, but states no coverage types, limits or additional insured parties. The solution assumes standard public-entity coverage with limits confirmed at negotiation. If the City requires limits or coverages the bidder does not carry, the cost is unplanned or the bidder cannot sign. The requirement is mandatory but the coverage terms are absent, and the solution's position is an assumption rather than a confirmed insurability.

Ten-year pricing and 180-day validity lock in costs before scope is known. The solution prices software subscription and maintenance for Years 1 through 10 and holds the price valid for 180 days, with every line carrying a stated assumption. Long-horizon subscription pricing plus a fixed implementation price, set before the Requirements document is fully analysed, leaves little room to absorb user-count growth, module additions or third-party interface costs without margin erosion. The RFP requires ten-year pricing and 180-day validity, and the solution prices against an unseen Requirements document with user counts fixed at 130 named and 85 concurrent financial users and 400 FTEs and 744 W2s.
